Over many years of teaching social work at various universities I began to notice that students increasingly had very little idea about the subject or why they wanted to study it. Many of them would look perplexed when I asked why they were enrolled. I have had responses like: "I thought it might be interesting, sort of"; "my gran told me I should do it"; and "it's like feeding people in homes, isn't it?"
Some said that they "simply had to come to uni" because there were no jobs, while others had "heard that the social work course was easy because it was practical". Of course there is a wider context that many so-called universities are dumping grounds for the unemployed, barely literate and demotivated, where they are taught by mediocre academics.
Last week Sir Martin Narey published his independent review on the education of children's social workers. His 18 recommendations included observing university teaching, scrutinising entry standards, examining the curriculum, auditing the rigour of examinations and other forms of student assessment, and evaluating practice placements. He also proposed relaxing the requirement for social workers to have placements in contrasting service settings, to allow those intent on a career in children's social work to spend all 170 days of placement in a children's setting.
His report was based on private interviews with employers, academics, students and social workers. His hope is that, if implemented, his recommendations will "significantly increase the confidence we can have in the initial training, and therefore the calibre, of newly qualified social workers".
I have done my own interviews with student and newly qualified social workers, and many of my findings concur.
Many of the students I interviewed were somewhat dismissive of the quality of their education. One told me: "I don't think any of the tutors really know who any of us are really. I turn up at a lecture, then I go home and that's it really."
Many also questioned the abilities of some of their peers, with one saying: "There are a few people on the course that I wonder how they got through the admissions interview in the first place."
The majority interviewed struggled with aspects of social science, especially sociology. One said: "I thought sociology was completely useless. I failed to see the direct relation to social work. We did ten weeks of sociology, six weeks of safeguarding adults and six weeks of safeguarding children. When you compare the two I would have thought there would have been more importance on safeguarding than useless sociology."
But unlike Narey, the majority appeared to understand the link between children's social work and adult dysfunction and, unlike him, they saw the need for diverse placements. One student observed: "In childcare, we have so many parents who are either misusing drugs or alcohol but we don't have any training that teaches us what that means or how that affects people. If you've never had any experience of drug abuse, and you've never had it in your placement, how are you going to know what to do?"
Nearly all of the students I interviewed would concur with Narey over the need to ensure appropriate (and high quality) practical placements. One said: "Lots of people were in family centres and day care centres that weren't meeting enough of their standards and in no way prepared them for front line social work."
The student added: "I think one person ended up in a children's home which didn't have any children in it. All she did was watch television and play on the computer."
Once on placement, or newly qualified, dissatisfaction with the quality of their education was soon forgotten because other nightmares were at hand, namely the spectre of poor IT provision, increased bureaucracy and multidisciplinary working. It is, of course, irrefutable that since the 1970s when individual decision-making, relative autonomy and individual creativity were valued, social work has increasingly become both bureaucratised and deskilled.
One student told me: "The team I was working in had to work alongside or work in partnership with education, health and housing services. What a nightmare. No one talks to each other. No one communicates with each other."
Another student said: "I spend about 75% of my time on the computer. I currently have to update two databases. It's all duplicated nonsense. The amount of money wasted on IT is absolutely incredible."
So, there is much for Narey to ponder. And there is a wider context.
Social and economic inequalities continue to blight the life-chances of huge numbers of individuals, families and communities. It's undeniable that there still exists a somewhat rigid social class system, with very little inter-generational social mobility and, almost inevitably, a widening of the gap between rich and poor, the haves and have-not's. It is the unemployed, the disaffected, the low paid and the working classes who are the primary and core recipients of social work involvement. Social work clients tend not to be found on the playing fields of Eton or Fettes, or the classrooms and changing rooms of Roedean or Benenden.
Social work students should be admitted to degree courses on the basis of a transparent and demonstrable commitment to social justice. Additionally, much of the social science content of degree courses should be eliminated. Clients require social workers well-acquainted with the availability of resources, agency procedures, and interpersonal sensitivity, not social scientific conundrums  however inherently interesting or intellectually demanding.

"There are so many songs we've done together, me and Patrick. I'm just so happy that I'm with him and he's with me," Hnath said.
On stage under the lights, it's their time to shine.
"It's probably the best kind of feeling for me," Lah said.
Lah and Hnath are just two members of Band Together Pittsburgh. The organization gives people on the autism spectrum the platform to perform.

Unlike the blue whale, today's largest animal, Hupehsuchus was modest in size, about three feet (one meter) long. It possessed a long and narrow snout, toothless mouth, front and back limbs that could serve as paddles for steering, and a broad tail that it flipped from side to side for forward propulsion.
Long and loose bones made up its snout, with a narrow lower jaw only loosely connected to the rest of the skull to let it open its mouth widely to take in large quantities of water bearing small prey called zooplankton.
The blue whale and its relatives have baleen plates composed of keratin - the substance that makes up our fingernails - in their mouth to strain out food such as shrimp-like krill from seawater.
Baleen does not lend itself well to fossilization and none was found in the Hupehsuchus fossils. But the researchers identified grooves and notches along the edges of its jaws suggesting the presence of soft tissues that could have served like baleen.

They are the ocean’s gentle giants, sweeping up clouds of tiny prey with a mouthful of living sieves. Yet blue whales and their baleen kin were not the first to wield this astonishing filter-feeding strategy. Long before whales ruled the seas, a small, strange reptile was already sipping the ocean like a living strainer.

Fresh fossils from China’s Hubei Province reveal that Hupehsuchus nanchangensis, a curious marine reptile that patrolled Triassic waters 248 million years ago, likely fed much like modern baleen whales during a riot of evolutionary experimentation after Earth’s worst mass extinction.

Forget titanic scale. Unlike the blue whale, today’s largest animal, Hupehsuchus stayed compact at about three feet (one meter) long. It brandished a long, narrow snout and a toothless mouth, with front and back limbs that acted like paddles for deft steering, and a broad tail it flicked side to side for thrust.

Its snout was built from long, loose bones, and its narrow lower jaw was only loosely tethered to the skull, freeing it to gape wide and gulp great volumes of water teeming with zooplankton. The setup screams specialization.

Modern baleen whales deploy plates made of keratin—the same stuff as human fingernails—to sift shrimp-like krill and other morsels straight from seawater. Those plates form nature’s grandest sieve.

But baleen is notoriously reluctant to fossilize, and none turned up in the Hupehsuchus specimens. Instead, scientists found grooves and notches tracing the jaw edges—tell-tale signs of soft tissues that may have worked like baleen without leaving a trace.

“Altogether, this points to a soft pouch made of skin around the mouth and throat, as in modern baleen whales, and some kind of filtering device hanging from the jaws, like baleen – but the ‘baleen’ and skin are not preserved,” said paleontologist Mike Benton of the University of Bristol in England, a co-author of the research published on Monday in the journal BMC Ecology and Evolution.

“Hupehsuchus nanchangensis would have continuously filter-fed at slow swimming speeds, from dense patches of plankton at the surface or in shallow water. It ingested water and prey together into its mouth, filtered out the water using a sieve, like baleen, and then swallowed the food,” added paleontologist Long Cheng of the Wuhan Center of China Geological Survey, the study’s lead author.

It is a feeding routine that mirrors modern bowhead and right whales, which cruise with mouths agape near the surface, combing out small prey from the brine in effortless sweeps.

This anatomy is a dramatic case of convergent evolution—the evolutionary echo that causes distant lineages to invent similar solutions. Wings sprouted in birds, bats and the extinct pterosaurs; here, a reptile and mammals arrived at the same watery strategy through separate paths.

“The further the relationship between two animals, the more fascinating this phenomenon becomes,” Cheng said. “Baleen whales are mammals and Hupehsuchus are reptiles. Their affinity is so distant. And they appeared more than 200 million years apart,” Cheng said.

The stage for this unlikely innovation was set by catastrophe. Runaway global warming sparked by massive Siberian volcanism shattered life at the end of the Permian Period, wiping out perhaps 90% of Earth’s species. Then came the rebound—rapid, exuberant, and opportunistic—as survivors surged into emptied niches and marine reptiles seized the seas.

Hupehsuchus first surfaced in the scientific record in the 1970s, but early fossils skimped on critical skull details. The new research showcases two newly uncovered specimens with beautifully preserved heads, finally opening a window onto how this pint-sized pioneer fed.

And Hupehsuchus is hardly alone in turning water into food. Today, whale sharks—the ocean’s largest fish—use their gills as sieves to trap drifting fare. Deep in the past, two other marine reptiles, Paludidraco about 230 million years ago and Morturneria about 70 million years ago, also appear to have filtered their meals. Going back even further, the armored giant Titanichthys, more than 100 million years older than Hupehsuchus, is perhaps the earliest known vertebrate to try the trick.

“Hupehsuchus perhaps could be the smallest-known vertebrate filter-feeder,” Cheng said.

The standard model reveals that apparently different phenomena are really different aspects of the same thing (radioactive decay and electricity are linked, for example). Thus it is that the world we see, with all its diversity and complexity, is made out of just a handful of elementary particles hopping around according to some simple rules.
Underpinning all of this is the notion of "symmetry". It is symmetry that allows us to specify the rules that constrain the behaviour of the particles and it is the presence of symmetry that often moves physicists to speak of beauty. Symmetry implies that there are underlying patterns in nature that constrain the way particles behave. Knowing the symmetries in nature is key to explaining how the particles move around.

But there is a huge fly in the ointment because the simplest realisation of the symmetries does not allow particles to have any mass. Scientists have found a way to create mutant organisms more reliably, using a recently developed gene-editing technique known as CRISPR. And just as in the "X-Men" movies, not everyone is happy about that.
The procedure, known as mutagenic chain reaction, is described in a paper published online Thursday by the journal Science. It uses genetic engineering to put a specific mutation in both copies of a gene associated with a particular trait. That gets around a cellular mechanism that usually keeps recessive mutations from being expressed.
Here's the classic, if overly simplistic, example: Children inherit sets of chromosomes from each of their parents, with each chromosome containing the genes for various traits. A blue-eyed child has to inherit the blue-eyed gene from both the mother and the father. Otherwise, the dominant brown-eyed gene trumps the recessive blue-eyed gene.
In reality, eye color is determined by more than one gene. But the same principle applies to genetic defects such as muscular dystrophy: Even if you inherit the mutated gene for muscular dystrophy from one parent, the normal gene from the other parent can compensate and keep you from getting the disease.
The downside for genetic engineers is that the mechanism makes it harder to introduce desired mutations. Mutagenic chain reaction, or MCR, makes the job easier. The researchers behind the Science study tweaked the CRISPR genome-editing procedure in fruit flies to make a mutation that's generated on one copy of a chromosome spread automatically to the other copy. Thus, both copies of the gene carry the mutation.
"MCR is remarkably active in all cells of the body, with one result being that such mutations are transmitted to offspring via the germline with 95 percent efficiency," study lead author Valentino Gantz, a graduate student at the University of California at San Diego, said in a news release.

UCSD Professor Ethan Bier, the paper's co-author, said the technique has "several profound consequences." It could accelerate the pace of genetic research, and facilitate the rapid dispersal of genetically engineered traits.
